Both concern errors in how participants were assigned
Assignment errors are selection problems within a study; these two biases concern what reaches the literature.
Both are removed by a larger sample size
A bigger sample reduces chance but does nothing about results that are never published or partly reported.
B.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 45

B.io: Discuss bias in cohort studies
B.q: Why is the generalizability of a prognosis study often limited?
opts: Its follow-up is always too short
Follow-up may be adequate; the limit arises from who the study patients are.
Its outcomes cannot be measured
Outcomes such as survival can be measured; the limit concerns who was studied.
Its patients were always randomized
Randomization deals with bias between groups but does not make the patients representative of other populations.
Its patients may not represent others
Correct: they may also not represent an individual patient, so how similar they are to yours must be judged.
B.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

B.io: Discuss the principles of community screening programs
B.q: A program urges smokers to stop. Which objective does it serve?
opts: Find disease so treatment prevents complications
That objective concerns disease such as hypertension, not a habit.
Find disease so treatment can cure it
Curative screening seeks disease itself, such as cancers, rather than changing a habit.
Change a behavioral risk factor
Correct. Trying to get people to stop smoking is the standard example of targeting a behavioral risk factor in order to change the behavior.
Change a metabolic risk factor
The metabolic example is diet aimed at lowering cholesterol, which is not smoking.
B.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

B.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
B.q: What does validity mean for a test?
opts: Its ability to determine correctly who has the disease
Correct, and it is measured by sensitivity and specificity. Reliability, by contrast, is getting a similar result when the test is repeated under the same conditions.
Its ability to change the post-test probability
That is what the likelihood ratio describes rather than what validity means.
Its cost relative to the gold standard
Cost is a consideration when ordering a test rather than a component of its accuracy.
Getting a similar result on repetition
That is reliability, also called precision, which says nothing about whether the result is right.
B.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

B.io: Compare and contrast the following study designs: cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, randomized controlled clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analysis
B.q: What is the ecologic fallacy?
opts: Applying individual data to a whole population
The fallacy runs in the other direction, from aggregate to individual.
Measuring exposure and outcome at the same time
Simultaneous measurement is a general feature of cross-sectional work rather than the fallacy named.
Assuming an association proves causation
Confusing association with causation is a separate error from the specific problem of aggregate data.
Applying aggregate data to an individual
Correct, and it is the standing hazard of ecologic data: a relationship that holds between populations need not hold within any one person in them.
B.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

B.io: Discuss the purposes of research
B.q: What is the purpose of exploratory research?
opts: To address a new or understudied topic and satisfy curiosity
Correct, and it has two further purposes that are practical rather than intellectual: testing the feasibility of a more careful study and developing the methods that study would use.
To attempt to explain why something occurs
That is explanatory research, which goes beyond describing what is happening to account for it.
To analyze data that another researcher has already collected
That describes secondary research, a distinction about the source of the data rather than the purpose of the study.
To observe carefully and describe what is found
That is descriptive research, which reports disease rates and the demographic characteristics of those affected.
B.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

B.io: Discuss methods to measure outcomes
B.q: What do near-identical five-year survival rates fail to show?
opts: How many patients were studied
The sample size is reported separately from the rate and is not what the rate conceals.
When the deaths occur
Correct: conditions such as a dissecting aneurysm, lung cancer and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis can share one five-year rate while their survival curves differ greatly.
Which patients had the disease
The rate is calculated for patients who have the disease; what it conceals is when the deaths happen.
Whether the disease exists
The rate presumes the disease exists; it does not describe the timing of deaths within the five years.
B.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

B.io: Compare and contrast the following study designs: cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, randomized controlled clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analysis
B.q: In which direction does a case-control study look?
opts: Forward, from an assigned intervention to outcome
Assignment of an intervention by the investigator describes a randomized controlled trial.
Backward, from outcome to exposure
Correct: participants are sorted by whether the outcome is present, and each group is then examined for whether the risk factor was present beforehand.
At a single moment, with neither before the other
Simultaneous measurement of risk factor and disease describes a cross-sectional study.
Forward, from exposure to outcome
Looking forward from exposure to outcome describes a cohort study rather than a case-control study.
B.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

B.io: Discuss following concepts and how they apply to medical research: Hypotheses, Sampling, Treatment, Comparative effectiveness, Clinical trials, Inclusion and exclusion criteria, Placebo, Randomization, Compliance, Blinding, Efficacy and effectiveness
B.q: Which is a recognized source of treatment hypotheses?
opts: Epidemiologic studies
Correct, alongside the mechanism or etiology of the disease, clinical observation, and trial and error.
A single coincidental recovery
Coincidence is one of the things treatment decisions should avoid resting on; hypotheses come from mechanism, clinical observation, epidemiology and trial and error.
A comparison of biased groups
Biased comparisons mislead rather than generate sound hypotheses; the recognized sources are disease mechanism, clinical observation, epidemiologic studies and trial and error.
Hope that a new drug works
Wishful thinking is a named hazard, not a source; hypotheses arise from mechanism, clinical observation, epidemiologic studies and trial and error.
B.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

B.io: Describe the various research methods utilized in medical research
B.q: Which instruments are used in primary research?
opts: Questionnaires, surveys, measurements and lab results
Correct, and what they have in common is that the investigator generates the data rather than drawing on data someone else has already collected.
Published guidelines and expert consensus statements
Those synthesize existing evidence rather than serving as data collection instruments.
Disease registries maintained by state governments
Registry data already exists, so analyzing it is secondary research.
Meta-analyses and systematic reviews
Those are examples of secondary research rather than instruments for collecting new data.
B.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 3

B.io: Discuss the concepts of validity and reliability and their relationship to measurement
B.q: Which question tests the content validity of a depression screening scale?
opts: Does the scale give the same score on a second administration?
Consistency across administrations is reliability rather than validity.
Does a high scorer have the affect of a depressed person?
That is a criterion validity question, comparing the score against an observable response.
Would a clinician interviewing the patient reach the same conclusion?
That is a construct validity question, comparing the measure with another measure of the same phenomenon.
Are the items representative of accepted symptoms of depression?
Correct, and the sample items make it concrete: sadness lasting more than two weeks, irritability and difficulty sleeping.
B.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 54

B.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
B.q: What effect does awareness of an epidemic have?
opts: It reduces the true incidence of the disease
Awareness changes detection rather than how many people actually fall ill.
It converts an epidemic into a pandemic
What makes an outbreak a pandemic is how widespread it becomes, not how well known it is.
It has no effect on case finding
Easier diagnosis of new cases is precisely the effect described.
It can make new cases easier to diagnose
Correct, with early COVID-19 as the example. It is also a reason measured frequency can rise partly because clinicians started looking.
B.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

B.io: Explain confounding variables and methods for controlling confounding
B.q: In a study of coffee drinking and pancreatic cancer, smoking is more common among coffee drinkers and also raises cancer risk. What role does smoking play?
opts: The outcome
The outcome is the cancer being studied; smoking is an additional factor rather than the disease itself.
An effect modifier
An effect modifier changes the size of the exposure's effect and is not a bias; smoking here is linked to both exposure and outcome.
A confounder
Correct: smoking is related to both the exposure, coffee, and the outcome, cancer, so it can produce a false association, a systematic error.
The exposure
The exposure under study is coffee drinking; smoking is an additional factor linked to both exposure and outcome.
B.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

B.io: Define criteria to determine causation
B.q: Before concluding that an association is causal, what must be excluded?
opts: Temporality, strength and analogy
Those are also criteria supporting cause; the explanations to exclude are bias, chance and confounding.
Bias, chance and confounding
Correct, taken in that order: bias in selection or measurement, then chance, then confounding, and only if none explains it is a cause likely.
Precision, power and validity
Those are properties of a study rather than the alternative explanations an association must be freed of.
Dose-response, reversibility and specificity
Those are criteria that SUPPORT a causal relationship, not alternative explanations to be excluded.
B.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

B.io: Discuss conflict of interest
B.q: What happens after peer reviewers recommend acceptance?
opts: The authors repeat the study
Repeating the study is not part of the process; acceptance is followed by editorial review and then publication.
It is published with no further review
An editorial review of language and grammar still takes place between acceptance and publication.
Peer reviewers correct the grammar
Language and grammar are checked by editors after acceptance rather than by the peer reviewers.
Editors review language and grammar
Correct, and only then is the article published; peer review as a whole helps to counter conflict of interest.
B.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

B.io: Describe advantages and disadvantages of screening exams
B.q: A program finds mostly slow-growing cancers, and screened patients appear to outlive unscreened patients whose cancers were found by symptoms. Which bias best explains this?
opts: Attrition bias
Attrition means participants dropping out, and the scenario is about the type of disease detected.
Compliance bias
Compliance bias arises because screened people are more invested in their health, which is not what this scenario describes.
Length-time bias
Correct. Screening catches more slow, favorable conditions, so the screened group looks better even if screening changed nothing.
Lead-time bias
Lead-time bias arises from earlier diagnosis of the same disease, not from detecting a different mix of slow and fast disease.
B.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

B.io: Describe cohort studies and the advantages and limitations of this type of study design in medical research
B.q: Which is an advantage of cohort studies?
opts: Incidence can be established directly
Correct, because following exposed and unexposed persons forward shows how many develop disease; exposure is also recorded without knowledge of the outcome.
Results are available within weeks
Cohort results may not be available for many years, since the group must be followed until the outcome occurs.
Rare diseases can be studied cheaply
Rare diseases need a very large cohort, so cohort studies are inefficient and expensive for them; case-control studies suit rare disease.
Few participants need enrolling
A large cohort must be enrolled, which is why cohort studies are inefficient.
B.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

B.io: Discuss the various types of bias in medical research including: selection/sampling bias, measurement bias, confounding, procedural bias, attrition effect, non-response bias, reporting bias, publication bias
B.q: Why might a sponsoring company contribute to publication bias?
opts: It selects participants who are most likely to benefit
Choosing favorable participants would produce selection bias within a study rather than bias in what gets published.
It insists that all its funded studies be published in full
Publishing everything would counteract publication bias rather than contribute to it.
It requires investigators to disclose conflicts of interest
Disclosure is a protection against threats to objectivity rather than a driver of publication bias.
It is less likely to support research unfavorable to its product
Correct, and it sits alongside journal editor preference as the second force keeping results that show nothing out of the literature.
B.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

B.io: Analyze resources for bias and validity
B.q: What did the retracted vaccine and autism study demonstrate about undeclared interests?
opts: The study was retracted purely because others could not replicate it
Failure to replicate was not the stated basis; the undeclared payment, the patent and serious ethical breaches were.
The conflict was declared but judged unimportant
The author failed to declare the payment, which is what made it a conflict rather than a disclosure.
An undisclosed payment and a competing patent lay behind the work
Correct: the author had been paid to advise lawyers representing parents, and had filed a patent for a competing vaccine without disclosing either.
Peer review reliably prevents this kind of failure
The paper passed peer review and was published in a major journal, which is precisely why the case is cautionary.
B.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

B.io: Discuss internal and external validity
B.q: What is noted about determining external validity?
opts: It is determined by the journal in which the study appears
Where a study is published says nothing about whether its findings generalize to other populations.
It follows automatically once internal validity is established
Results can be entirely correct for the sample studied and still not hold in a different clinical setting.
It is established by the size of the sample alone
A large sample improves precision but does not by itself show that findings transfer to other settings.
It is rarely determined from a single study
Correct, and the practical consequence is that a result has to be reproduced in other settings and populations before it can be relied on outside the original one.
B.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51

B.io: Discuss variation, distribution, and dispersion in data
B.q: What is the weakness of the mean?
opts: It cannot be calculated for interval data
Interval data is exactly what a mean is calculated from, so this is not what limits the measure.
It ignores the number of observations
The number of observations is the divisor, so it is central to the calculation.
It is the same as the mode in all distributions
They coincide in a symmetric distribution but diverge when the distribution is skewed.
It can be affected by extreme outliers
Correct, which is why the median, defined by position rather than magnitude, holds up better when a few values sit far from the rest.
B.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 71

B.io: Explain the following statistical concepts: Significance, P value, Null hypothesis, Confidence interval, Statistical power, Multiple comparisons, Multivariable modeling
B.q: How is the probability of an event estimated from counts?
opts: Times it does not occur divided by times it can occur
That is the probability that the event does NOT occur, the complement of the one being estimated.
Times it occurs divided by times it can occur
Correct, and the result must lie between zero, meaning the event cannot occur, and one, meaning it will definitely occur.
Times it occurs divided by times it does not occur
That ratio is the odds rather than the probability; a probability puts the occurrences over ALL the opportunities, occurrences included.
Times it can occur divided by times it occurs
Inverting the fraction gives a value of one or more, but a probability can never exceed one.
B.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

B.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
B.q: What does a likelihood ratio above 10 indicate?
opts: Moderate evidence to rule in
Moderate evidence to rule in corresponds to the 5 to 10 band rather than to ratios above 10.
An indeterminate result
The indeterminate band runs from 0.5 to 2, where a result barely shifts the probability at all.
Strong evidence to rule in
Correct, with 5 to 10 giving moderate evidence to rule in, and the band from 0.5 to 2 being indeterminate.
Strong evidence to rule out
Ruling a disease out strongly requires a ratio below 0.1 rather than one above 10.
B.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 44

B.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
B.q: Which is an epidemiologic function of surveillance?
opts: Publishing systematic reviews of the literature
Evidence synthesis is a separate activity from population surveillance.
Setting the price of preventive services
Setting the price of services is not among the epidemiologic functions of surveillance that are named.
Detecting outbreaks and epidemics

Correct, alongside determining the magnitude of a problem, understanding natural history, documenting geographic spread, testing etiologic hypotheses, evaluating control strategies and monitoring changes in an agent.
Assigning treatment to individual patients
Treatment of individuals is clinical work rather than a surveillance function.
B.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

B.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
B.q: Which of these is a suggested way to keep current?
opts: Sales representatives
Sales representatives have a commercial interest, and are not among the suggested sources, which are organizations, journals, colleagues and patients.
Advertising
Advertising is promotion rather than appraised evidence, and the suggested sources are organizations, journals, colleagues and patients.
Patients
Correct, and the others suggested are professional organizations, journal articles and colleagues.
Press releases
Press releases summarize results without appraisal; suggested sources are professional organizations, journals, colleagues and patients.
B.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

C.io: Discuss following concepts and how they apply to medical research: Hypotheses, Sampling, Treatment, Comparative effectiveness, Clinical trials, Inclusion and exclusion criteria, Placebo, Randomization, Compliance, Blinding, Efficacy and effectiveness
C.q: Why is random assignment preferred when testing a treatment?
opts: It limits systematic differences between groups
Correct: cohort comparisons are limited by systematic differences in groups other than the treatment factor, which random assignment is used to limit.
It removes the need for a comparison group
Trials still depend on comparison groups, such as treatment versus placebo; random assignment makes those groups comparable rather than unnecessary.
It ensures every participant complies
Randomization does not control behavior; compliance is the degree to which participants act in accordance with instructions and can fail for many reasons.
It keeps participants unaware of their group
Keeping participants unaware of their treatment is blinding, a separate safeguard from randomization, which decides who is assigned to which group.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

C.io: Identify epidemiologic data sources
C.q: How is epidemiology defined?
opts: The study of disease mechanisms at the cellular and molecular level
That describes pathophysiology. Epidemiology works at the level of populations rather than mechanisms within an individual.
The statistical analysis of data collected during a single clinical trial
Statistical analysis is a tool epidemiology uses, not its definition, and epidemiology extends far beyond any one trial.
The distribution and determinants of health-related states in populations

Correct, and the definition does not stop at studying: it extends to applying that study to the control of health problems, which is what makes it a practical discipline rather than a descriptive one.
The study of how drugs are absorbed, distributed and eliminated
That describes pharmacokinetics. Epidemiology concerns the distribution and determinants of health states across populations.
C.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

C.io: Discuss conflict of interest
C.q: A trade group's guideline endorses only products sold by its member companies. Which conflict of interest is this?
opts: Intellectual conflict of interest
Intellectual conflict sits with personal biases and career interests of authors, not with benefit to one organization.
Financial conflict of interest
Financial conflict concerns funding and personal gain for authors or their families rather than benefit to an organization.
Personal conflict of interest
Personal conflicts involve an author's own biases and career, not the interests of a sponsoring organization.
Institutional conflict
Correct, because institutional conflict arises when a recommendation benefits one organization more than others.
C.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32

C.io: Compare and contrast the following study designs: cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, randomized controlled clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analysis
C.q: How should the comparison group in a cohort study be chosen?
opts: At random from the general population
Random selection from the population would not ensure similarity on everything except the exposure.
To match the exposed group on outcome
Matching on outcome would defeat the purpose, since outcome is what the study is trying to observe.
As similar as possible except for the exposure
Correct, because any other difference between the groups becomes an alternative explanation for whatever difference in outcome appears.
To be as different as possible from the exposed group
Differences other than the exposure are exactly what make a comparison uninterpretable.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

C.io: Discuss bias in cohort studies
C.q: What is susceptibility bias?
opts: One group's outcomes are more likely to be detected
That is measurement bias, which arises from how the outcome is classified and detected.
The assembled groups differ in ways that affect outcome
Correct: for example the groups may be at different points in the disease course, have other concurrent disease, or have had prior treatment.
Patients drop out or change groups
That is migration bias, which arises during follow-up rather than in how the groups were assembled.
Results apply only to a narrow population
That concerns generalizability, which is limited when study patients are not representative of other populations.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

C.io: Discuss the various types of bias in medical research including: selection/sampling bias, measurement bias, confounding, procedural bias, attrition effect, non-response bias, reporting bias, publication bias
C.q: In a medication trial, the placebo control group turns out to be older on average than the experimental group. What does this represent?
opts: Measurement bias in recording age
Nothing suggests age was measured wrongly; the problem is that it differs systematically between the groups being compared.
Attrition effect
Attrition describes participants dropping out during the study rather than a baseline difference between the groups.
Age acting as a confounding variable
Correct, because age is plausibly associated with both group membership and the outcome, so its effect cannot be separated from the effect of the medication being tested.
Reporting bias by the investigators
Reporting bias concerns withholding a subset of data rather than an imbalance in a baseline characteristic.
C.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 43

C.io: Differentiate between the types of variation in disease measurement
C.q: A patient's blood pressure differs between two readings taken at different times of day. Which variation does that illustrate?
opts: Random measurement error
Random error has equal probability of falling above or below the true value rather than following a known condition.
True biologic variation from unknown random factors
Biologic variation is the residual scatter left when conditions are held the same, not the effect of a known one.
Interobserver variation
Only one patient and one measurement condition differ here; no second observer is involved.
Systematic variation, since the condition is known to affect it
Correct: time of day is a known condition of measurement affecting the value, alongside position, smoking beforehand and the white coat phenomenon.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 64

C.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
C.q: Why is mortality listed as a surveillance strategy?
opts: Mortality rates are the most accurate measure of disease
Accuracy is not the argument; the point is that death is sometimes the first moment a case becomes visible.
Mortality determines the case definition
The case definition is established during the investigation rather than derived from deaths.
Some cases are detected only at death
Correct, which makes death certification a genuine source of case finding rather than merely a record of outcome.
Deaths are easier to count than cases
Ease of counting is not the reason given; detection of otherwise unrecognized cases is.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

C.io: Describe cohort studies and the advantages and limitations of this type of study design in medical research
C.q: What must a cohort study have so that attrition does not falsely skew the outcome?
opts: A larger control group
A larger control group does not replace participants who are lost; the safeguard is complete follow-up of everyone in the cohort.
Recall of past exposures
Recall of past exposure is a concern in case-control studies; in a cohort, losses are prevented by following everyone over time.
Random assignment to exposure
Exposure is observed rather than assigned in a cohort study; dropout is addressed by following everyone through to the outcome.
Complete follow-up of the cohort
Correct: if participants drop out, the outcome data can be falsely skewed, so the cohort must also be followed long enough to observe the expected outcome.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

C.io: Discuss the principles of community screening programs
C.q: Which objective fits a program that screens for hypertension?
opts: Change a behavioral risk factor
Getting people to stop smoking is the example of a behavioral target, not hypertension.
Find disease so treatment can cure it
Curing applies to conditions such as sexually transmitted infections and cancers, whereas hypertension is managed to avoid complications.
Change a metabolic risk factor through diet
A diet change to lower cholesterol is the metabolic example, whereas hypertension is treated to prevent complications.
Find disease so treatment prevents complications
Correct. Treating hypertension prevents its complications, unlike screening for conditions where treatment can cure.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: Discuss variation, distribution, and dispersion in data
C.q: What is the interquartile range?
opts: The variability of scores about the mean
The variability of scores about the mean is the standard deviation rather than a range between percentiles.
The full spread from lowest to highest value
That is the range, which the interquartile range exists to improve on.
A limited range index, such as the 25th to 75th percentiles
Correct, and limiting it that way is the point: it describes the spread of the bulk of the data without being dictated by the two extreme values.
The proportion of values within one standard deviation
That proportion is about two thirds in a normal distribution, which is a different statement.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 73

C.io: List considerations for treatments or interventions that undergo controlled trials
C.q: What must participants give to take part in a trial?
opts: Proof they can comply with instructions
Compliance is not a precondition that participants must prove; the ethical requirement is that they give consent to take part.
Knowledge of which group they are in
Knowing the group would defeat blinding; the ethical requirement is consent to take part, given before entering the trial.
Consent to take part
Correct: participants must give consent, which is one of the conditions for an ethical trial alongside genuine uncertainty about the treatments.
A promise not to withdraw
Ethical trials rest on consent, not on binding participants to stay; consent to take part is what participants must give.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

C.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
C.q: Which criterion in the modified Centor score can score minus one?
opts: Absence of cough
Absence of cough scores one point, as do fever, tender nodes and tonsillar findings.
Age over 45
Correct: ages 3 to 14 score one point, 15 to 44 score nothing, and over 45 scores minus one, because the infection becomes less likely with age.
Tonsillar swelling or exudate
Tonsillar swelling or exudate scores one point, like fever, absent cough and tender nodes.
Temperature above 38 degrees
A temperature above 38 degrees scores one point, like the other three clinical criteria.
C.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

C.topic: Type I and type II error
C.io: Explain the following statistical concepts: Significance, P value, Null hypothesis, Confidence interval, Statistical power, Multiple comparisons, Multivariable modeling
C.q: Which study limitation can produce a type II error?
opts: A p value smaller than 0.001
A p value that small is a significant result, which is the opposite of the not significant result that defines a type II error.
Short follow-up or poor compliance
Correct: too brief a follow-up or subjects not adhering can hide a real difference, so the result looks not significant though it is a false negative.
Blinding the investigators
Blinding reduces bias; it does not by itself hide a true difference, whereas study limits such as follow-up length can.
Random assignment of participants
Random assignment is a strength of design that balances the groups; it does not cause a real difference to be missed.
C.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: Discuss the use of common databases to access medical literature
C.q: What does the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report carry?
opts: Original randomized controlled trial reports
Primary trial reports appear in research journals indexed in Medline rather than in this publication.
Systematic reviews of therapeutic questions
Systematic reviews are found in the Cochrane Library and similar resources.
Individual state disease registry data
Registry data is collected by state governments rather than published as recommendations here.
Public health policies for prevention and treatment
Correct, and it sits among the guideline sources alongside the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and the Task Force on Community Preventive Services.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

C.io: Describe case control studies and the advantages and limitations of this type of study design in medical research
C.q: What does a case-control study not need to do that a cohort study does?
opts: Ask about earlier exposure
Earlier exposure is exactly what the study asks about, which is why recall bias is a concern.
Define who counts as a case
A case group must still be defined as persons who have the condition; that is the starting point of the design.
Identify a comparison group
The control group without the condition is required, since exposure in cases is compared with exposure in controls.
Wait for the condition to develop
Correct, since the cases already have the condition, which is why results do not take years to obtain.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

C.io: Discuss the various types of bias in medical research including: selection/sampling bias, measurement bias, confounding, procedural bias, attrition effect, non-response bias, reporting bias, publication bias
C.q: A trial compares surgical with medical therapy. Patients in the surgical arm were healthy enough to tolerate an operation, while the medical arm carried more comorbidities. Which bias does this illustrate?
opts: Non-response bias
Non-response bias arises when survey respondents differ from those who do not reply, which is not the situation described.
Publication bias
Publication bias concerns whether studies reach print according to their results rather than how participants were assigned within one study.
Selection bias
Correct. The groups differ in baseline health as well as in treatment, so a difference in outcome cannot be attributed to the therapy, which is the defining problem of biased sampling.
Measurement bias
Measurement bias would arise from how the outcome was assessed rather than from a difference in who was allocated to each group.
C.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 40

C.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
C.q: For a question comparing two diagnostic tests, which outcome fits?
opts: Number of tests ordered
Test volume describes practice patterns rather than how accurately a test detects the disease of interest.
Sensitivity and specificity
Correct, because a question about how well a test detects disease can name the accuracy of each test, expressed as sensitivity and specificity, as its outcome.
Length of the clinic visit
Visit length is a process measure and does not show whether either test identifies disease more accurately.
Patient satisfaction with the result
Satisfaction is a patient-reported result and does not measure whether a test correctly separates those with and without the disease.
C.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

C.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
C.q: How should a screening campaign combine tests?
opts: Screen with a highly sensitive test, confirm with a highly specific one
Correct, because the first pass should miss as few cases as possible and the second should avoid committing healthy people to further investigation.
Screen with a highly specific test, confirm with a sensitive one
That order would discard cases at the first step, which is what screening is meant to avoid.
Use two tests of equal sensitivity
The strategy deliberately pairs complementary properties rather than duplicating one.
Use the gold standard for screening
Gold standard tests tend to be expensive, invasive and not easily completed, which makes them unsuitable for screening.
C.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

C.io: Discuss survival analysis
C.q: What does survival analysis calculate when people enter at various times?
opts: The random error of each measurement
Random error is estimated statistically; the follow-up contributed by each person is measured in person-years.
The sensitivity of the outcome measure
Sensitivity describes test accuracy, not the follow-up time contributed by each person.
The prevalence at a single moment
Prevalence is a snapshot at one time and does not account for how long each person was followed.
The person-years each person contributes
Correct: people can be added at different points in their disease and each contributes the time they are followed.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

C.io: Describe the various research methods utilized in medical research
C.q: What is study design?
opts: The organization and plan for data collection and analysis
Correct, and it matters because it bears directly on the validity and reliability of the data: strong design gives strong data, and strong data gives valid conclusions.
The number of participants enrolled
Sample size is one element of a design rather than the design itself.
The clinical question the study sets out to answer
The question comes first; the design is the plan built to answer it.
The statistical tests applied once data exist
Analysis is part of the plan, but design is the whole organization of collection and analysis rather than the tests alone.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

C.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
C.q: Which considerations apply when ordering a diagnostic test?
opts: Repeat every abnormal test at least twice
Repeating a test without an indication is specifically something to avoid.
Risk against benefit, the test's limits, and its cost
Correct, alongside two instructions: avoid ordering tests indiscriminately, and avoid repeating a test without an indication.
Order the most sensitive test available in every case
Sensitivity and specificity are inversely related, so which matters depends on the clinical question.
Order every test the patient requests
Indiscriminate ordering is named as the first thing to avoid.
C.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

C.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
C.q: How does prevalence help in clinical reasoning?
opts: It identifies which test is most accurate
Test accuracy is a property of the test, although prevalence does change how its result should be read.
It prioritizes the differential diagnosis
Correct: think horses, not zebras. It also affects the interpretation of test results, because it sets the pretest probability.
It establishes the cause of the condition
Prevalence measures how much of a condition is present rather than what produces it.
It determines the severity of the condition
Severity is measured by case fatality rather than by how common a condition is.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

C.io: Analyze resources for bias and validity
C.q: What marks a quality source of medical information?
opts: Publication within the last twelve months
Currency matters and appears in the website appraisal method, but peer review is what marks the source as a quality one.
A large number of citations to the article
Citation counts reflect attention rather than the scrutiny a source received before publication.
Endorsement by a pharmaceutical company
Commercial sponsorship is a reason for caution, since sponsors are less likely to support unfavorable findings.
Peer review, with government databases a further category
Correct, and the matching warning is blunt: be cautious of websites, which carry no equivalent guarantee of scrutiny before publication.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

C.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
C.q: To which kinds of questions is grading of evidence most often applied?
opts: Treatment and screening
Correct, and grading is a quick way to assess clinical significance, although it still involves some value judgment in weighing pros and cons.
Anatomy and staging
Grades summarize evidence for action and apply mainly to treatment and screening.
Prevalence and incidence
These describe how common disease is; grading recommendations targets decisions about what to do, such as treatment and screening.
Etiology and disease naming
Grading concerns recommended actions, and is most often used for treatment and screening rather than for these topics.
C.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

C.io: Discuss the concepts of rate and rate determination
C.q: What does the crude mortality rate measure?
opts: Deaths among those diagnosed with a disease
That is case fatality, which measures the severity of a disease rather than mortality in a population.
Deaths from one specified cause in a population
That is the cause-specific mortality rate, which narrows the numerator to a single cause.
Deaths from all causes in a population
Correct, which is why it is called crude: it makes no adjustment for the age structure of the population, and an older population will show a higher figure for that reason alone.
Deaths within a particular age group
That is the age-specific mortality rate, which narrows both numerator and denominator to one age band.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

C.io: Discuss the principles of community screening programs
C.q: What evidence should exist before screening is introduced?
opts: That screening alters the natural history of disease
Correct. The classic statement asks for conclusive evidence that screening changes the natural history in a significant proportion of those screened.
That most people would accept screening
Acceptability matters, but the evidence needed is about changing the course of disease.
That screened people live longer after diagnosis
Longer survival after diagnosis may be lead time alone and does not prove screening changes the disease course.
That the test detects any abnormality
Detecting abnormalities is not enough, and it may even lead to overdiagnosis and incidentalomas.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

C.io: Discuss factors that impact or influence disease measurement
C.q: Why is the age-adjusted death rate the right measure for comparing a county with its state?
opts: It counts only deaths among residents
Residency affects who is counted rather than whether the comparison is fair between different age structures.
It uses live births as the denominator
Live births are the denominator of the infant and maternal mortality rates rather than of adjusted death rates.
It removes differences in age structure between the two
Correct, and without it a county with an older population would appear less healthy on the crude rate for that reason alone.
It expresses each cause as a percentage of deaths
That describes proportionate mortality rather than an age-adjusted rate.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

C.io: Compare and contrast the following study designs: cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, randomized controlled clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analysis
C.q: What kind of design is a randomized controlled trial?
opts: Experimental, for testing hypotheses
Correct, because the investigator assigns and manipulates the intervention rather than observing an exposure that arose on its own.
Descriptive, for characterizing a single group
Descriptive designs are case reports and case series rather than trials.
Observational, for testing hypotheses
Observational designs watch an exposure rather than assigning it; the randomized trial assigns.
Observational, for generating hypotheses
Hypothesis generation without assignment describes the cross-sectional design.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

C.io: Discuss intervention in terms of prevention
C.q: Which is a component of the burden of suffering from a condition?
opts: Test sensitivity
Sensitivity describes how well the screening test finds disease, so it is part of test quality rather than burden.
Test simplicity
Simplicity belongs to the quality of the screening test, not to the burden the condition causes.
Disability
Correct. Death, disease, disability, discomfort, dissatisfaction and destitution are the components of burden, together with measures such as hospitalizations and incidence.
Treatment cost-effectiveness
Cost-effectiveness belongs to the criterion about treatment, not to the burden of suffering.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

C.io: Describe considerations for disease surveillance and outbreak investigations
C.q: Why must an investigation confirm that an epidemic truly exists?
opts: An apparent rise may reflect detection rather than occurrence
Correct, which is why a baseline and a settled case definition come first: both awareness and definition change how many cases are found.
Epidemics are always reported by clinicians first
How a rise first comes to attention does not settle whether the rise is real rather than an artifact of detection.
Endemic disease cannot produce clusters of cases
Endemic disease can produce apparent clusters, which is part of why confirmation is needed.
Attack rates cannot be determined otherwise
The attack rate is determined as part of the same investigation rather than depending on the confirmation.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

C.io: Discuss methods to measure outcomes
C.q: What does five-year survival measure?
opts: Percent of patients whose disease returns within five years
That is the recurrence rate, which counts a return of disease after a disease-free interval.
Percent of patients alive five years from a point in their disease
Correct, and the starting point is some point in the course of the disease, which is why where that point falls matters.
Percent of a population dying of the disease in five years
That describes disease-specific mortality, whose denominator is the population rather than patients.
Percent of patients cured after five years of treatment
Survival counts patients who are alive, not cured; a patient can be alive with disease at five years.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: Discuss the purposes of research
C.q: Which clinical question does the term Diagnosis address?
opts: How does treatment change the course of the disease?
That is Treatment, which asks what an intervention does once disease is established.
Does early detection improve the course of the disease?
That belongs to Prevention, which covers both keeping disease from arising and detecting it early.
What conditions lead to the disease?
That is Cause, which concerns the origins of the disease rather than the accuracy of the tests used to detect it.
How accurate are the tests used to identify the disease?
Correct. The question is about the performance of the tests themselves, which is why test properties are studied as a topic in their own right rather than assumed.
C.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

C.io: Describe the various research methods utilized in medical research
C.q: Which designs are observational?
opts: Cohort and case-control
Correct, because in both the investigator watches an exposure that occurred independently rather than allocating it. The randomized trial is the experimental example.
Meta-analyses
A meta-analysis pools existing studies rather than observing or assigning anything itself.
Quasi-experimental studies
In a quasi-experimental study the researcher still controls the treatment, though not the assignment to groups.
Randomized controlled trials
In a randomized trial the investigator assigns and manipulates the intervention, which makes it experimental.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

C.io: Define criteria to determine causation
C.q: How is strength of association judged in a causal assessment?
opts: By whether a mechanism is known
That is biologic plausibility, whether the relationship makes sense biologically.
By whether exposure can be reversed
That is reversibility, in which decreased exposure leads to less disease.
By the size of the relative risk
Correct: a large relative risk is a strong association, which makes a causal relationship more likely.
By how many studies report it
That describes consistency, meaning findings are replicable in other studies, rather than strength.
C.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

C.io: Describe prognosis
C.q: How can the natural history of a disease be changed to improve prognosis?
opts: Through longer observation alone
Watching a disease without acting describes its natural history rather than changing it; only an intervention can alter the course.
Through more precise measurement
Better measurement improves how outcomes are described but does nothing to change what happens to the patient.
Through larger study cohorts
A larger cohort makes an estimate more precise; it does not change the disease course, which requires an intervention.
Through clinical intervention
Correct, and the further aim is to detect disease at an earlier point so that treatment is as effective as it can be.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

C.io: Describe prognostic factors
C.q: What do prognostic factors identify?
opts: Patients with the same disease but different prognoses
Correct, which is what makes them useful: they separate patients who share a diagnosis into groups that fare differently.
Patients with different diseases and equal prognoses
Prognostic factors work within one disease, separating patients who have it into better and worse outcomes.
Healthy people who will develop the disease
That is the job of risk factors, which predict who becomes ill rather than how ill patients fare.
Tests that confirm a diagnosis
Confirming a diagnosis is the job of diagnostic tests; prognostic factors predict the outcome once the disease is known.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

C.io: Describe advantages and disadvantages of screening exams
C.q: Which conditions does screening tend to detect, giving rise to length-time bias?
opts: Conditions that are never diagnosed
Conditions that are never diagnosed are not what defines the bias; it arises because screening over-detects slow conditions relative to rapid ones.
Conditions with no prognostic difference
The bias exists because slow and fast conditions do differ in prognosis.
Slow, favorable-prognosis conditions
Correct. Slow conditions are present for longer, so a screen is likely to catch them, and they carry better prognoses than fast ones.
Rapid conditions with poor prognoses
Rapid conditions usually produce symptoms before the next screening, so they tend to escape it.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

C.io: Describe randomized controlled trials and the advantages and limitations of this type of study design in medical research
C.q: In a trial, 12 of 200 patients on a new drug and 30 of 200 on placebo had the outcome. What is the relative risk on the new drug?
opts: That is the placebo group's own risk, 30 divided by 200; relative risk is the new-drug risk divided by it, 0.06 divided by 0.15, or 0.4.
Correct: the risk on the new drug is 12/200 = 0.06 and on placebo 30/200 = 0.15, and 0.06 divided by 0.15 is 0.4.
That inverts the ratio, placebo risk over new-drug risk; relative risk here puts the new-drug risk of 0.06 over the placebo risk of 0.15, giving 0.4.
That is the risk in the new-drug group alone, 12 divided by 200; relative risk compares the two groups' risks, 0.06 divided by 0.15.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: Explain the following statistical concepts: Significance, P value, Null hypothesis, Confidence interval, Statistical power, Multiple comparisons, Multivariable modeling
C.q: Below what p value is a result generally accepted as statistically significant?
opts: Correct, meaning a chance of about 1 in 20; a p value of 0.01 (1 in 100) is generally called highly significant and 0.001 (1 in 1000) very highly significant.
The generally accepted cutoff is stricter than 0.10; a value below 0.05 is what is usually called statistically significant.
A p value below 0.01 is generally called highly significant, which is a stricter grade above the ordinary 0.05 cutoff.
A p value of 0.5 means the chance explanation is 50/50, which is nowhere near the accepted threshold of 0.05.
C.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

C.io: Analyze resources for bias and validity
C.q: Why are higher-level studies more likely to show that an outcome is due to what was studied?
opts: They are least vulnerable to bias
Correct. Systematic error is what allows something other than the exposure or intervention to produce the observed outcome, so reducing it strengthens the attribution.
They enroll patients from a single center
Restricting recruitment to one center tends to reduce generalisability rather than strengthen the attribution of outcome to cause.
They report larger effect sizes
A large effect can still be produced by bias; what matters is how vulnerable the design is to systematic error.
They are published in higher-impact journals
Where a study appears does not determine whether its outcome can be attributed to the factor being studied.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

C.io: Discuss the principles of evidence-based medicine
C.q: What does the validity step of evidence-based practice assess?
opts: Whether the outcome improved after the change
That is the final step, evaluating performance or outcome after the change has been made.
Whether the question was correctly framed
Framing the question is the first step rather than what the validity assessment examines.
Whether the research applies to this patient
Applying the search results to individual patient encounters is the next step, after validity has been judged.
Whether the research is true
Correct, and it comes before application rather than after: research whose truth has not been established should not be carried into a patient encounter.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

C.io: Discuss the limitations of differentiating between normal and abnormal
C.q: What does statistical abnormality not necessarily imply?
opts: That the value lies outside the reference range
Lying outside the range is what statistical abnormality means rather than something it fails to imply.
Practical or clinical abnormality
Correct, with a serum cholesterol of 201 as the example: above the desired level, but not clinically significant in itself.
That the value was measured accurately
Measurement accuracy is a separate question from what an accurate abnormal value means.
That the test was performed correctly
Technical performance is a separate issue from the interpretation of a correctly obtained result.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 75

C.io: Discuss the concepts of validity and reliability and their relationship to measurement
C.q: What does reliability mean?
opts: The measurement is free of systematic error
Freedom from systematic error is validity; reliability concerns consistency, and a measure can be consistently wrong.
The measurement captures what it is meant to
Capturing what the measurement is meant to capture is validity, also called accuracy, rather than reliability.
The result applies to other populations
That is external validity of a study rather than reliability of a measurement.
Repeated attempts produce similar results
Correct, and it goes by several other names: reproducibility, repeatability and precision. Note that none of them implies the result is correct.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 58

C.io: Analyze resources for bias and validity
C.q: Which two situations both earn a Grade B?
opts: High certainty of substantial benefit only
That single situation defines Grade A, where the benefit is substantial and the certainty about it is high.
High certainty of moderate benefit, or moderate certainty of more
Correct, and either way the instruction is the same as for Grade A: offer or provide the service.
Insufficient evidence to weigh benefits against harms
That is Grade I, where evidence is lacking, poor or conflicting, so the balance of benefits and harms cannot be determined.
Moderate certainty of a small benefit only
That describes Grade C, where the service is offered selectively.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 12

C.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
C.q: A test has a positive likelihood ratio of 4. What does that mean?
opts: Four percent of positive results are correct
The ratio is a multiplier on the odds rather than a percentage of correct results.
The odds of the condition are multiplied by four
Correct: a likelihood ratio multiplies the odds of the condition rather than its probability, so a ratio of 4 makes the odds four times what they were before the test.
The test is correct four times out of five
A likelihood ratio does not express a rate of correctness; it expresses how much the result multiplies the odds of the condition.
Four patients in every hundred have the disease
Four patients per hundred having the disease would be a prevalence rather than a likelihood ratio.
C.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

C.io: Explain confounding variables and methods for controlling confounding
C.q: Which method gives each patient an equal chance of falling into either group?
opts: Stratification
Stratification compares rates within subgroups with otherwise similar probability of the outcome, and is applied in the analysis phase.
Matching
Matching selects comparison patients with the same characteristics as each patient in the other group rather than assigning by chance.
Restriction
Restriction limits the range of characteristics of patients in the study rather than assigning them by chance.
Randomization
Correct: it is applied in the design phase and spreads confounders between the groups by chance.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

C.io: Discuss following concepts and how they apply to medical research: Hypotheses, Sampling, Treatment, Comparative effectiveness, Clinical trials, Inclusion and exclusion criteria, Placebo, Randomization, Compliance, Blinding, Efficacy and effectiveness
C.q: Which factors does effectiveness take into account?
opts: Compliance, practicality and cost
Correct: these real-world factors are what separate effectiveness, in ordinary circumstances, from efficacy, in ideal circumstances.
Dose, half-life and mechanism of action
Those are pharmacologic properties of a drug; effectiveness takes into account compliance, practicality and cost.
Randomization, blinding and allocation
Those are design features of a trial; effectiveness takes into account compliance, practicality and cost.
Age, sex and diagnostic category
Those are participant characteristics that may define strata; effectiveness takes into account compliance, practicality and cost.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

C.io: Compare and contrast the following study designs: cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, randomized controlled clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analysis
C.q: What distinguishes a cross-sectional ecologic study?
opts: It uses population rather than individual level data
Correct, relating the frequency of a characteristic to an outcome of interest across populations rather than within individuals.
It measures each participant twice
Repeated individual measurement describes a longitudinal design rather than an ecologic one.
It follows individuals forward over many years
Following individuals forward describes a cohort study, which uses individual rather than population level data.
It assigns an exposure to half the population
Assignment of exposure makes a study experimental, and nothing is assigned in an ecologic study.
C.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18

C.io: Discuss the purposes of research
C.q: Which three inputs combine to produce good clinical decision making?
opts: External evidence, statistical significance and journal reputation
Significance and reputation are features of evidence rather than separate inputs, and this omits both clinical expertise and the patient.
Clinical expertise, institutional policy and cost containment
Policy and cost are practical constraints rather than the three named inputs, which are expertise, external evidence and the patient's own values.
Patient values, provider confidence and peer consensus
Confidence and consensus are among the alternative influences named, not the inputs to evidence-based decision making.
Clinical expertise, external evidence, and patient values
Correct, and the output named is not merely a decision but improved patient care, which is the point of combining all three rather than relying on any one.
C.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: Describe observational studies and the advantages and limitations of this type of study design in medical research
C.q: What makes observational treatment studies hard to interpret?
opts: Confounding and effect modification
Correct: both are difficult to avoid when treatment is not assigned, so differences may reflect other factors rather than the treatment.
The absence of any real-world patients
Observational studies do include real-world patients, which is a benefit; the difficulty is avoiding confounding and effect modification.
Use of blinding that hides the exposure
Blinding is not the defining problem; confounding and effect modification are difficult to avoid in observational studies.
Excessive control over who receives treatment
Observational studies lack the investigator's control over who receives treatment; that lack is what makes confounding hard to avoid.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

C.io: Interpret relative risks and odds ratios
C.q: In a cohort 2x2 table with exposed cases (a), exposed noncases (b), unexposed cases (c) and unexposed noncases (d), which expression gives the relative risk?
opts: ad divided by bc
That is the odds ratio, the measure of association for case-control studies rather than the relative risk of a cohort.
a/(a+b) divided by c/(c+d)
Correct: the incidence in the exposed, a over a plus b, divided by the incidence in the unexposed, c over c plus d.
a/(a+c) divided by b/(b+d)
That divides within columns, comparing the proportion exposed among cases with that among noncases, which is how a case-control table is read.
a/c divided by b/d
That is the odds ratio written another way (equal to ad over bc); relative risk uses the incidences a/(a+b) and c/(c+d).
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

C.io: Discuss the impact of study design on the ability to determine causation
C.q: Why does random assignment strengthen causal conclusions?
opts: It guarantees a significant result
Random assignment does not guarantee statistical significance, which depends on the true difference and the study's power.
It makes measurements more reliable
Reliability of measurement is a separate property that depends on the measuring method, not on how groups are assigned.
It balances confounders between the groups
Correct: random assignment spreads confounding factors evenly, although random error remains and is still accounted for through p values.
It removes all random error from results
Random error is never eliminated; it is estimated statistically and reflected in the p values.
C.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

C.io: Identify different levels of measurement in data
C.q: Which is an example of ordinal data?
opts: Blood group
Blood group has categories with no inherent order, which makes it nominal.
Cancer staging from I to IV
Correct, alongside pitting edema graded one to four plus, patient status or condition, and the drug risk categories for birth defects.
Number of heart attacks
A count has defined equal intervals and takes only specific values, which makes it discrete interval data.
Blood pressure
Blood pressure has order and defined equal intervals, which makes it interval and continuous.
C.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 50

C.io: Explain the following statistical concepts: Significance, P value, Null hypothesis, Confidence interval, Statistical power, Multiple comparisons, Multivariable modeling
C.q: A study makes 60 comparisons between groups, none reflecting a true difference. If significance is set at a p value of 0.05, about how many will appear significant by chance?
opts: That doubles the expected number; 60 comparisons at 1 in 20 gives 3 by chance alone.
Correct: a p value of 0.05 corresponds to a chance of 1 in 20, and 60 divided by 20 is 3.
With none of the differences real, the only significant results are chance ones, and at 1 in 20 about 3 are expected among 60.
That treats half of the comparisons as significant, whereas a threshold of 0.05 corresponds to only 1 in 20.
C.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

C.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
C.q: What does parallel testing generally increase?
opts: The prevalence of the disease
Prevalence is a property of the population rather than something a testing strategy alters.
The reliability of each individual test
Reproducibility of a single test is unchanged by how it is combined with others.
Specificity and positive predictive value
Those are what serial testing maximizes, at the cost of sensitivity.
Sensitivity and negative predictive value
Correct, so disease is less likely to be missed. How much sensitivity improves depends on how well each test catches the cases the other misses.
C.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

C.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
C.q: Which topic suits a narrative review better than a systematic review?
opts: An overview of many aspects of a disease
Correct, because narrative reviews suit broad topics and a range of issues, whereas a systematic review needs a focused question.
Whether one drug lowers mortality more than another
A focused comparison of two treatments on one outcome is the kind of specific, predetermined question a systematic review is built to answer.
Whether screening lowers deaths in one age group
This names a population, an intervention and an outcome, so it is a focused question that a systematic review can answer.
Whether a new test detects a disease more accurately
A question about the accuracy of one test is specific and answerable, which is the setting for a systematic review of test studies.
C.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

C.io: Discuss methods of predicting risk
C.q: In an individual patient, what is the best predictor of disease?
opts: Presence of a single risk factor
A risk factor raises the probability for groups of people; in an individual, early clinical disease is the better predictor.
The relative risk of the exposure
Relative risk describes the strength of an association in groups, not what will happen to one person, for whom early clinical disease predicts best.
Presence of early clinical disease
Correct: risk factors raise the probability of disease, but in an individual it is early clinical disease itself that predicts best.
Incidence in the wider population
Incidence in a population gives a probability for the group; for an individual patient the best predictor is early clinical disease.
C.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

C.io: Describe number-needed-to-treat (NNT) and number-needed-to-harm (NNH)
C.q: The number needed to harm for a side effect is 200. If 1,000 patients receive the intervention, how many are expected to be harmed?
opts: 200,000 patients
That multiplies 1,000 by 200; the number treated must be divided by the number needed to harm, giving 5.
200 patients
That repeats the number needed to harm itself, whereas it is the number of patients treated per one harmed.
5 patients
Correct. The number treated divided by the number needed to harm is 1,000 divided by 200, which is 5 patients harmed.
0.2 patients
That divides 200 by 1,000, which is the wrong way round; dividing 1,000 by 200 gives 5.
C.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

C.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of systemic reviews
C.q: A reader asks how the studies in a systematic review were located. Which question belongs with it?
opts: Were the tables printed in color?
Presentation style does not bear on validity; the reader needs to know how studies were found, selected and judged.
Which inclusion and exclusion criteria were used?
Correct, because how studies were found and which criteria decided their entry are read together with how valid the original studies were.
How many pages does the reference list run?
Length of the reference list is not an appraisal criterion; the question is whether the criteria for including studies were explicit.
Which reviewer wrote the discussion section?
Who drafted a section says nothing about the quality of the review; appraisal concerns the search, the criteria, and the original studies.
C.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

D.io: Compare and contrast incidence and prevalence rates
D.q: What does incidence describe?
opts: Everyone who has the condition at one moment
That is prevalence, which counts existing cases as well as new ones.
The distribution of a condition by person and place
Distribution describes where and in whom disease occurs rather than how fast new cases appear.
The proportion of cases that prove fatal
That is case fatality, a measure of severity rather than of new occurrence.
New cases arising in previously healthy people
Correct, over a specified time period. That restriction to the previously healthy is what separates it from prevalence, which counts everyone who has the condition.
D.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

D.io: Discuss following concepts and how they apply to medical research: Hypotheses, Sampling, Treatment, Comparative effectiveness, Clinical trials, Inclusion and exclusion criteria, Placebo, Randomization, Compliance, Blinding, Efficacy and effectiveness
D.q: A drug works well in a tightly monitored trial where nearly everyone takes every dose, but poorly in clinics where many patients miss doses. How do its efficacy and effectiveness compare?
opts: Efficacy is low and effectiveness is high
That reverses them; the ideal circumstances of the trial give high efficacy, and the poor real-world performance is low effectiveness.
Both efficacy and effectiveness are low
Efficacy is judged under ideal circumstances, and the drug works well there, so efficacy is high; effectiveness is what falls short.
Efficacy is high and effectiveness is low
Correct: efficacy reflects ideal circumstances, such as full compliance, while effectiveness reflects ordinary circumstances, including missed doses.
Both efficacy and effectiveness are high
Effectiveness reflects ordinary circumstances, including compliance, and the drug performs poorly there, so effectiveness is low.
D.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

D.io: Compare and contrast statistical significance and clinical importance
D.q: Which pairing best contrasts statistical and clinical significance?
opts: Random error versus systematic error
That contrasts two sources of error in a study, not the two kinds of significance.
Validity versus reliability of a test
Those are properties of measurement, not the two kinds of significance.
Precision versus accuracy of measurement
Precision and accuracy describe measurement quality, not the difference between statistical and clinical significance.
Chance versus relevance to patients
Correct: statistical significance asks how likely chance is as an explanation, while clinical significance asks whether the difference matters to practice.
D.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

D.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
D.q: What determines how much parallel testing improves sensitivity?
opts: How well each catches what the other misses
Correct: two tests that fail on the same patients add little, whereas complementary tests between them catch far more of the cases.
The prevalence of the disease
Prevalence affects predictive values rather than how complementary two tests are.
How expensive the tests are
Cost bears on which strategy is chosen rather than on how much sensitivity improves.
How specific each test is
Specificity governs false positives, whereas the gain being described is in case detection.
D.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

D.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
D.q: A clinical question asks whether nebulized hypertonic saline, compared with normal saline, shortens hospital stay in infants with bronchiolitis. Which element is the outcome?
opts: Length of hospital stay
Correct, because the outcome is what one hopes to accomplish, measure, improve or affect, here how long the infants remain in the hospital.
Nebulized hypertonic saline
That is the intervention, the main treatment under consideration, rather than the result the investigators want to measure.
Normal saline
Normal saline is the comparison, the alternative against which the intervention is judged, rather than the outcome.
Infants with bronchiolitis
That is the patient or population element: the group of patients the answer is meant to apply to, not the result being measured.
D.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

D.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
D.q: What limits the diagnosis of disease?
opts: The prevalence of the disease alone
Prevalence shapes what a result means but is not what limits diagnosis in general.
How good the tests used to measure it are
Correct, and the rest follows from it: sensitivity and specificity guide test selection, while predictive values describe what a given result means.
The number of tests ordered
Ordering more tests does not overcome the limits of the tests themselves, and indiscriminate ordering is to be avoided.
The cost of the gold standard
Cost affects which tests are practical rather than setting the limit on diagnosis.
D.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 51

D.io: Compare and contrast the following study designs: cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, randomized controlled clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analysis
D.q: What is a systematic review built to answer?
opts: As many related questions as the literature allows
The question a systematic review answers is specific and focused rather than as broad as the literature allows.
How common a condition is at one moment
Prevalence at a moment is measured by a cross-sectional survey.
A specific, focused question
Correct, and it does so by systematically identifying and evaluating multiple studies rather than by surveying a field impressionistically.
Whether an assigned intervention works
Assigned interventions are tested by randomized trials; the review synthesizes such studies.
D.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

D.io: Differentiate between the types of variation in disease measurement
D.q: What is intraobserver variation?
opts: A flaw in the measuring instrument
An instrument flaw is systematic measurement error rather than observer variation.
One patient's value changing between measurements
That is intrasubject variation, arising from the patient rather than the reader.
One observer interpreting the same thing differently twice
Correct, with a radiologist reviewing the same radiograph at two different times and reaching different interpretations as the example.
Two observers interpreting the same thing differently
Two observers reading the same finding differently is interobserver variation rather than variation within one reader.
D.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 60

D.io: Describe the various research methods utilized in medical research
D.q: What lies at the start of the trajectory toward evidence-based information?
opts: Ideas, from observation, biology and reasoning
Correct, and they become hypotheses, then observational studies, then experimental studies, and only then evidence-based information. Imagination is named alongside them.
Case reports
Case reports feed the process, but the trajectory begins with ideas drawn from observation, biology, reasoning and imagination.
Randomized controlled trials
Experimental studies sit near the end of the trajectory rather than at its start.
Systematic reviews
Syntheses come after the studies they appraise, at the far end of the trajectory.
D.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

D.io: Analyze resources for bias and validity
D.q: In the pyramid, which design sits immediately below randomized controlled trials?
opts: Systematic reviews
Systematic reviews sit above randomized controlled trials, at the apex of the pyramid.
Cohort studies
Correct, and case-control studies with case series and reports sit below those in turn, so the order rises from case reports through case-control and cohort to randomized trials.
Case-control studies
Case-control studies sit below cohort studies rather than immediately below randomized trials.
Expert opinion
Expert opinion sits at the base of the pyramid, several levels below randomized trials.
D.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

D.io: List considerations for treatments or interventions that undergo controlled trials
D.q: What should happen if evidence of harm, futility or effectiveness emerges during a trial?
opts: The sample size is quietly reduced
Shrinking the sample does not answer evidence of harm, futility or effectiveness; the study is ended when such evidence appears.
Enrollment continues to the planned end
Carrying on regardless would keep participants exposed to harm or deprive them of a proven benefit; the study is ended when such evidence appears.
Only the control group is stopped
